title: ‘Sold a Story’ Season 2: Teachers and Schools Matter. We Should Act Like It. d-act-like-it/
author: Conor P. Williams
summary: Conor P. Williams reflects on the launch of the second season of Emily Hanford's Sold a Story podcast, which shifts from early reading to the larger question of what happened to teaching. He recalls the impact of the first season, which pushed dozens of states to align literacy instruction with the science of reading. The new season marshals evidence from high-poverty Houston schools, Illinois pedagogical experiments, Zig Engelmann's Direct Instruction, HighScope and the largely forgotten Project Follow Through. Williams predicts the season will launch a thousand takes and be conscripted into proxy fights over charters and No Child Left Behind. His own takeaway is that schools matter and students do better when educators teach more effectively, even though poverty and other structural forces also shape development. He hopes the series can rekindle political appetite for improving K-12 schools after years of avoiding structured reform.
points: Season two of Sold a Story broadens the question from how reading is taught to why proven instructional practices were abandoned by many schools.
Williams points to Project Follow Through, Direct Instruction and HighScope as forgotten evidence that better teaching can solve learning problems.
The first season shows how journalism can drive policy, since dozens of states changed laws to ground literacy instruction in the science of reading.
He warns the new season will be seized on for proxy battles over charters and accountability, obscuring its central point.
His message is balanced: structural forces like poverty matter, but so does school effectiveness, and both can be true.
quotes: The new “Sold a Story” season explores whether we know more about effective teaching than our schools generally show.
In other words, what if researchers identified general instructional practices that worked best for kids … but those practices were abandoned by many schools and teachers anyway?

And yet, the season’s real, insistent lesson is this: schools matter, and students do better when educators teach more effectively.
